questions.stem: About the plasma membrane:
options: It is about 70–100 nm thick
It separates the intracellular environment from the extracellular environment
It is a passive wall that lets all substances cross freely
Its glycoproteins and glycolipids act as a cellular "ID" that helps tell self from non-self
questions.explanation: The membrane is a thin (7–10 nm), dynamic, selective barrier — not a passive wall. Cell recognition relies on glycoproteins and glycolipids.

questions.stem: A patient with chest pain has a raised blood troponin. Which statements are correct?
options: Troponin I/T is the central biomarker of acute myocardial infarction
Cell injury disrupts the membrane and intracellular contents leak into the blood
Troponin is a non-specific marker of haemolysis
Troponin is the marker of rhabdomyolysis
questions.explanation: Membrane integrity is a diagnostic principle: injured cells leak their contents. Troponin = myocardial injury; LDH is the non-specific marker, CK/myoglobin the muscle (rhabdomyolysis) markers.

questions.stem: About membrane phospholipids:
options: Each has a hydrophobic head and two hydrophilic tails
Phosphatidylinositol is a precursor of the second messengers IP₃ and DAG
Phosphatidylserine is mainly in the outer leaflet
The hydrophobic core is a barrier to ions and polar molecules
questions.explanation: Phosphatidylserine is in the inner leaflet; its exposure on the outer surface is the "eat-me" signal of apoptosis. PC and sphingomyelin are the outer-leaflet phospholipids.

questions.stem: About the movements of membrane phospholipids:
options: Flip-flop usually requires enzymes such as flippases and scramblases
Rotation around the molecule's own axis is very rare
Lateral diffusion within a leaflet is fast
Flip-flop from one leaflet to the other is very frequent
questions.explanation: Lateral diffusion, rotation and flexion are fast; flip-flop is very rare because the polar head would have to cross the hydrophobic core.

questions.stem: Cholesterol in the plasma membrane:
options: Increases the membrane's permeability to ions
Its synthesis in the liver is reduced by statins, which inhibit HMG-CoA reductase
Limits excessive fluidity at high temperature and prevents solidifying at low temperature
Forms lipid rafts with sphingolipids
questions.explanation: Cholesterol buffers fluidity and decreases permeability to ions and small polar molecules. Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase → ↑ hepatic LDL receptors → ↓ circulating LDL.

questions.stem: About membrane proteins and the glycocalyx:
options: Blood groups are an example of glycocalyx-based recognition
Integral proteins are embedded in the bilayer, and many are transmembrane
The glycocalyx covers both faces of the membrane
Peripheral proteins cross the whole bilayer
questions.explanation: Peripheral proteins sit on one surface without crossing the bilayer. Sugar chains are found only on the outer surface.

questions.stem: About the three classes of membrane transport:
options: Primary active transport uses ATP directly (pumps)
Passive transport uses no ATP and goes down the gradient
Vesicular transport requires ATP
Active transport moves substances against their gradient
questions.explanation: Primary active transport uses ATP directly (pumps); secondary active transport uses the energy of an ion gradient. Vesicular transport needs ATP.

questions.stem: Which of the following cross the membrane by simple diffusion through the lipid bilayer?
options: Steroid hormones such as cortisol
Glucose
Na⁺ and K⁺ ions
O₂ and CO₂
questions.explanation: Simple diffusion concerns small, non-polar, lipid-soluble molecules (gases, steroids, vitamins A, D, E, K). Charged ions and large glucose need facilitated diffusion.

questions.stem: Which changes increase the rate of simple diffusion (Fick's law)?
options: A higher temperature
A thicker membrane
A larger molecule
A larger concentration gradient
questions.explanation: Rate ∝ surface × concentration difference × permeability / thickness. Permeability decreases with molecular size; thickening (fibrosis, oedema) slows diffusion.

questions.stem: About channels and carriers in facilitated diffusion:
options: Carriers are slower than channels
Channels form water-filled pores and are very fast
Channels saturate, reaching a maximal rate (Vmax)
Carriers bind the molecule and change shape to release it on the other side
questions.explanation: Saturation (Vmax when all carriers are busy) is a property of carriers; channels are rarely limiting and can pass millions of ions per second.

questions.stem: Which gate type — example pairs are correct?
options: Voltage-gated — Na⁺ channels of the nerve impulse
Mechanically gated — hair cells of the inner ear
Ligand-gated — nicotinic ACh receptor at the neuromuscular junction
Ligand-gated — touch receptors
questions.explanation: Touch receptors and hair cells are mechanically gated (stretch or pressure). Ligand-gated channels open when a specific molecule binds.

questions.stem: Insulin acts on a muscle cell after a meal. Which statements about glucose entry through GLUT4 are correct?
options: Glucose crosses GLUT4 through a water-filled pore
Insulin increases the number of GLUT4 carriers, so more glucose enters
Transport by GLUT4 can be saturated
GLUT4 moves glucose against its gradient using ATP
questions.explanation: GLUT carriers perform facilitated diffusion: down the gradient, no ATP, saturable and regulated (insulin ↑ GLUT4 in muscle and fat). Pores are a feature of channels.

questions.stem: Osmosis:
options: Moves water towards the side with less solute
Is the movement of water from the side with low solute concentration to the side with high solute concentration
Is fast through aquaporins, water channels that block ions and solutes
Requires ATP
questions.explanation: Osmosis is passive: water moves towards the higher solute concentration (less free water), slowly through the bilayer and rapidly through aquaporins.

questions.stem: A red blood cell is placed in a hypotonic solution:
options: 0.9 % NaCl is an example of such a solution
The cell shrinks (crenation)
The cell swells and may burst (haemolysis)
Water enters the cell
questions.explanation: Hypotonic = less solute outside: water enters, the cell swells and may lyse. Crenation occurs in hypertonic solutions; 0.9 % NaCl is isotonic.

questions.stem: During one cycle of the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase:
options: ATP hydrolysis phosphorylates the pump, which changes shape
3 Na⁺ bind to the pump on the inside
2 K⁺ bind to the pump on the inside
One net positive charge is moved out of the cell
questions.explanation: 3 Na⁺ bind inside → phosphorylation → Na⁺ released outside → 2 K⁺ bind outside → dephosphorylation → K⁺ released inside. 3 out / 2 in = one net charge out (electrogenic).

questions.stem: Roles of the Na⁺/K⁺ pump include:
options: Secreting gastric acid; it is blocked by omeprazole
Maintaining the Na⁺ and K⁺ gradients and the resting potential
Controlling cell volume
Creating the Na⁺ gradient used by secondary active transport
questions.explanation: The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase is inhibited by digoxin. Gastric acid comes from the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase of parietal cells, blocked by proton pump inhibitors (omeprazole).

questions.stem: About the primary active transporters:
options: SERCA pumps Ca²⁺ back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum so muscle can relax
The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase is inhibited by digoxin
The H⁺/K⁺-ATPase of gastric parietal cells is blocked by proton pump inhibitors
CFTR, a Cl⁻ channel of the ABC family, is defective in cystic fibrosis
questions.explanation: The H⁺/K⁺-ATPase is stimulated by histamine, ACh and gastrin and inhibited by somatostatin.

questions.stem: Secondary active transport (cotransport):
options: The Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger (NCX) is a symport
The Na⁺-K⁺-2Cl⁻ cotransporter (NKCC) is an antiport
Usually uses the Na⁺ gradient created by the Na⁺/K⁺ pump
The transporter itself does not use ATP, but stops working if the Na⁺/K⁺ pump stops
questions.explanation: Symport = same direction (SGLT, NKCC, Na⁺-amino acids); antiport = opposite directions (NHE, NCX).

questions.stem: In an intestinal cell absorbing glucose:
options: The basolateral Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase keeps intracellular Na⁺ low
The apical SGLT1 carries 2 Na⁺ with 1 glucose into the cell
Glucose leaves through basolateral GLUT2 by facilitated diffusion
Glucose exit at the basolateral membrane uses ATP directly
questions.explanation: One cell uses all three mechanisms: secondary active (SGLT1, apical), passive (GLUT2, basolateral) and primary active (Na⁺/K⁺ pump, basolateral).

questions.stem: About oral rehydration solution and gliflozins:
options: Gliflozins block SGLT2 and glucose reabsorption in the proximal tubule
Oral rehydration works because water is actively pumped into intestinal cells
Gliflozins block GLUT4 in muscle
Oral rehydration solution contains glucose and Na⁺ together because SGLT1 absorbs both and water follows by osmosis
questions.explanation: Water is never pumped: it follows the absorbed Na⁺ and glucose by osmosis. Gliflozins are SGLT2 inhibitors used in type 2 diabetes and heart failure.

questions.stem: About endocytosis:
options: Phagocytosis takes up extracellular fluid and dissolved solutes non-selectively
Receptor-mediated endocytosis uses clathrin-coated vesicles and is saturable
Phagocytosis is performed by neutrophils, macrophages and dendritic cells
Pinocytosis is non-selective
questions.explanation: Phagocytosis engulfs large solid particles after recognition; uptake of fluid and solutes is pinocytosis, done continuously by almost all cells.

questions.stem: A young patient has very high blood LDL because of a mutation of the LDL receptor:
options: Receptor-mediated endocytosis of LDL fails
The defect concerns phagocytosis
Cholesterol stays in the blood and causes early atherosclerosis
Hepatocytes normally take up LDL by receptor-mediated endocytosis
questions.explanation: Familial hypercholesterolaemia: the LDL receptor cannot mediate selective uptake (e.g. by hepatocytes), so LDL stays in the blood.

questions.stem: Exocytosis:
options: Regulated release is triggered by a rise in Ca²⁺
Removes membrane from the cell surface
Uses SNARE proteins for vesicle fusion
Includes insulin secretion by pancreatic β cells
questions.explanation: Exocytosis adds membrane to the cell surface (endocytosis removes it). Examples: neurotransmitter release, insulin, digestive enzymes.
